channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Taiwan's economy grew an estimated 13.72% in the first half on AI-driven exports, and Singapore lifted its 2026 growth forecast to 4.5–5.5% as electronics output jumped 88% — though its construction and consumer sectors are cooling.
item.description:
The AI investment wave is powering Asia's tech-heavy economies. Taiwan's first-half growth is estimated at 13.72%, driven by exports and private investment tied to AI, high-performance computing and cloud infrastructure; analysts argue the island's real edge is its ability to coordinate a dense supply network — chips, packaging, boards, power, cooling and assembly — into fast, reliable production, cementing its role as a critical technology hub. Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry raised its 2026 GDP forecast to 4.5–5.5% (from 2–4%), citing a strong first half (6.1% growth) and the global AI boom; its electronics sector grew 88% in the second quarter, lifting non-oil exports 18.6% — the strongest first-half showing since 2010. But the gains are uneven: Singapore's construction growth slowed sharply to 5.8% (from 12.9%), food-and-beverage services contracted, and the ministry flagged that supply disruptions from the Iran conflict are weighing on its chemicals cluster. Regional corporate profits, too, were led overwhelmingly by AI-linked sectors, with communications and IT profits up 109.8% and 69.4%.

Industry Impact

The AI-driven boom is a double-edged signal for ACS. On the upside, the electronics and semiconductor build-out is intensely materials-hungry — advanced packaging, chip assembly, thermal management and server/data-centre construction all consume specialty adhesives, encapsulants, thermal-interface materials and conformal coatings — so Taiwan and Singapore's surge points to strong high-value demand in the electronics ACS segment. On the downside, Singapore's explicit warning that the Iran conflict is hurting its chemicals cluster, plus its cooling construction sector, shows the broad-based, building-and-consumer ACS demand is still soft even where headline growth is high. The takeaway: chase the electronics-linked specialty opportunity, but don't mistake AI-led GDP for a broad recovery in construction-and-consumer ACS volumes.

Commercial Times | CNA | CNA | Lianhe Zaobao | Chinatimes

item.title: Britain sealed a breakthrough trade deal with the Gulf states, the EU tightened cross-border e-commerce with a €3 parcel fee and fines on Chinese platforms, and an Ifo survey found 88% of German firms rely on US digital providers.
item.description:
Several European trade-and-policy threads moved at once. The UK secured a trade deal with the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council — the first G7 country to do so — a breakthrough after long talks, spurred partly by the economic fallout of the Iran crisis. The EU tightened cross-border e-commerce: it imposed a fixed €3 tariff on incoming low-value parcels and scrapped the duty exemption for parcels under €150, fined Alibaba's AliExpress €550 million and accused Temu of obstructing an inspection — part of a global move (mirrored by the US, Thailand, Japan and Russia) to end "de minimis" low-value import loopholes. A Munich-based Ifo Institute survey underlined Europe's strategic vulnerability: nearly 88% of German companies use US digital products and services and 31% consider themselves highly dependent, yet few plan countermeasures. And in a step toward diversification of a different kind, China's central bank named Deutsche Bank the yuan-clearing bank in Frankfurt, aiming to expand renminbi use in the EU and deepen China–EU financial ties.

Industry Impact

These shifts reshape the trading and operating context for ACS producers in Europe. A UK–Gulf deal opens easier access to fast-growing Gulf construction and industrial markets — a bright spot for coatings and sealants demand — and to Gulf petrochemical feedstock links. Tighter EU e-commerce rules raise costs for the low-value import flows that carry some consumer adhesives and DIY products, nudging sourcing toward compliant regional supply. The Ifo dependence figure is a strategic flag: chemical firms' own digital and R&D stacks lean heavily on US providers, a resilience risk worth mapping. And a Frankfurt yuan-clearing hub could, over time, ease renminbi-denominated settlement for firms trading with Chinese suppliers and customers.

Arab News | CFLP | Handelsblatt | Global Times

item.title: Washington signalled it will resolve its tariff dispute over India's Russian-oil purchases, Thailand offered to leverage its military alliance in trade talks, and the US reaffirmed a $500 billion commitment to Southeast Asia.
item.description:
US trade diplomacy in Asia is intensifying, blending tariffs with security. White House trade adviser Peter Navarro said President Trump and Indian Prime Minister Modi have a "very good working relationship" and will resolve the dispute over threatened tariffs tied to India's purchases of Russian oil — a notable de-escalation signal, though Navarro repeated the US claim that India helped fund Russia's war by buying crude and re-exporting refined products. Thailand, facing higher US "forced-labour" tariffs, is preparing to use its military alliance as leverage: officials warn that steep tariffs could force Bangkok to scale back cooperation, including the long-running Cobra Gold exercises, while offering to cut its own tariffs and adopt US import standards for goods like beef and alcohol (Thailand ran a $51 billion trade surplus with the US in 2025). And the US ambassador to ASEAN, Kevin Kim, stressed continued security and economic engagement, noting the US has invested more than $500 billion in Southeast Asia — more than in China, India, South Korea and Japan combined — with over 6,000 American firms in the region.

Industry Impact

How these bargains land shapes the ACS demand map across Asia. A US–India tariff truce would steady one of the sector's fastest-growing markets and its export-manufacturing base. Thailand's leverage play highlights that the region's manufacturing hubs — automotive, electronics, appliances, all ACS-intensive — are negotiating from strength, and the outcomes will determine where production (and materials demand) concentrates. Washington's reaffirmed ASEAN commitment, set against China's parallel courtship of the bloc, means Southeast Asia stays a contested growth zone where both supply chains and material-supplier relationships are in play. For ACS makers, the read is that Asian manufacturing demand is resilient but its exact location is being redrawn by these tariff-and-security deals.

The Hindu Business Line | The Economic Times | The Straits Times | CNA

item.title: Russia's budget deficit rose 32% to about 6.5 trillion rubles ($79 billion) in seven months as oil-and-gas revenue fell; Ukraine says Putin is readying a large autumn call-up, and the Supreme Court barred the anti-war Yabloko party from September's vote.
item.description:
The war's fiscal and political costs are mounting for Moscow. Russia's federal budget deficit widened 32.3% year-on-year to 6.5 trillion rubles (about $79 billion), or 2.8% of GDP, in January–July — already far above the 3.79 trillion rubles planned for the whole of 2026 — as oil-and-gas revenue fell 16.8% (to $55.8 billion) under the US blockade and sanctions, even as spending rose 14.5%; the finance minister signalled the full-year target may be raised. Non-oil revenue rose 18.3%, showing how heavily the budget now leans on the domestic economy. Militarily, Ukrainian President Zelensky says Putin is preparing a large-scale mobilisation for autumn — immediately after September's parliamentary elections — potentially involving several hundred thousand recruits by year-end. Politically, Russia's Supreme Court banned the liberal, anti-war Yabloko party from those elections; the party will appeal, and commentators read the move as the Kremlin pre-empting any protest-vote rallying point ahead of the mobilisation.

Industry Impact

The direct ACS exposure is small — Russia is largely walled off from Western chemical trade — but the second-order effects are significant. A ballooning deficit and collapsing oil revenue show the blockade is grinding down Russia's war finances, which bears on how long the Hormuz disruption (and its feedstock-price effects) may last. A large autumn mobilisation would deepen and extend the conflict, sustaining the energy-price risk premium and the sanctions architecture that shape European feedstock and logistics costs. For chemical producers, the signal is that neither the war nor its cost pressures are near resolution — plan for the elevated-cost, high-uncertainty environment to persist into 2027.

Anadolu Agency | Interfax | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: India's first-quarter growth is tracking near 8% on State Bank of India estimates, above the central bank's 7%, and Fitch affirmed its BBB- rating for a 20th year as New Delhi prioritises critical minerals amid fresh China border friction.
item.description:
India remains the bright spot among large economies. State Bank of India's "nowcast" — a real-time estimate built from 54 high-frequency indicators — puts first-quarter FY27 growth at 8%, above the Reserve Bank of India's 7% projection, with 86% of its indicators accelerating. Fitch Ratings affirmed India's sovereign rating at BBB- (its lowest investment grade) with a stable outlook for a 20th straight year, praising a robust growth outlook and solid external finances while flagging risks from fiscal spending, youth job protests and higher oil prices from the West Asia war. India is now the world's sixth-largest economy at $3.92 trillion nominal GDP, per the IMF's April outlook, and is leaning into industrial policy: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal told parliament that energy, fertilizers, electronics, semiconductors, critical minerals, pharma and medical devices are priorities for supply-chain security, with critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, graphite and rare earths pushed in trade and FTA talks. The geopolitics are less settled: India's foreign ministry warned that renewed friction along the disputed China border is "the most serious" issue and could affect overall bilateral relations — even as Washington signals it will resolve its dispute over India's Russian-oil purchases (see other insight in this alert).

Industry Impact

India is one of the clearest structural growth markets for ACS demand — 8% growth, sustained public capex, PLI manufacturing incentives and infrastructure build-out translate into rising construction, automotive, electronics and packaging volumes that pull through adhesives, coatings and sealants. Fitch's stability underpins the investment case for local capacity. The critical-minerals push matters two ways: it secures inputs for the electronics and EV value chains ACS serves, and it signals India will bargain hard on raw-material access in trade deals. The China border friction is a watch-item — a sharper deterioration could disrupt the India–China industrial supply links that still feed Indian manufacturing.

Business Standard | LiveMint | The Economic Times | The Economic Times | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: Swiss Re put first-half disaster losses at $100 billion, with insured losses of $42 billion the lowest since 2020, yet warned risk is rising as the WMO flagged a severe El Niño and European food producers warned drought will lift prices.
item.description:
A quieter first half masks a rising trend. Swiss Re estimates global economic losses from natural disasters at $100 billion in the first half of 2026 — down about a third year-on-year and 10% below the ten-year average — with insured losses of $42 billion, the lowest for a first half since 2020, driven mainly by severe thunderstorms. But the insurer warns the lull hides a long-term rise in risk, and that losses typically climb in the second half with Atlantic hurricanes. The outlook is darkening: the World Meteorological Organization says a severe "Super El Niño" — an unusually strong Pacific warming that amplifies heatwaves, drought and storms — has formed, threatening farm output across Southeast Asia. In Europe, heat and drought are already biting: UK and continental food producers warn that hits to fruit, vegetable and grain supply will push food prices up into 2027, Austria is negotiating who pays €1 billion in farm damage, and Triodos Bank estimates the season could cost the EU around €180 billion (roughly 1% of GDP). Meanwhile typhoons White Dolphin/Dolphin and Chan-hom struck eastern China and Japan's Kanto region, triggering flood responses and insurance payouts.

Industry Impact

Weather risk feeds ACS through both demand and disruption. Reconstruction after storms, floods and fires is adhesive-, sealant- and coating-intensive, so an active second half could lift repair-and-rebuild demand — but the same events snarl logistics and raw-material flows (the low Rhine forcing Covestro's force majeure is the clearest current example). A Super El Niño that hits agriculture raises bio-based feedstock costs and food-price inflation, feeding the broader cost pressure squeezing chemical margins. And the long-term rise in heat and water stress is reshaping construction demand toward more durable, weather-resistant and energy-efficient materials — a structural opportunity for high-performance coatings and sealants even as near-term operations stay exposed to acute disruption.

Le Figaro | Daily Sabah | CNA | The Independent | Der Standard | Xinhua | China Economic Net

item.title: Global industrial-robot installations set records — about 542,000 in 2024 and 575,000 in 2025, heading past 700,000 by 2028 — while orders for China's Unitree humanoid-robot IPO ran roughly 8,300 times the shares offered.
item.description:
Automation is scaling fast on two fronts. The International Federation of Robotics reports about 542,000 industrial robots were installed worldwide in 2024 — more than double a decade earlier — with roughly 575,000 in 2025 and annual installs expected to top 700,000 by 2028 if current growth holds. The humanoid segment is drawing frenzied investor interest: China's Unitree aims to raise about 6 billion yuan in its listing, and retail investors ordered roughly 8,300 times the shares on offer. Chinese robotics is also pushing into Europe — Greece's Kefalos Technology is deploying Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots at solar plants, substations and logistics sites — and China's own clusters are growing, with Tianjin's intelligent-robot output reaching CNY 6.8 billion in the first half. Adoption is spreading beyond factories into supply-chain software: an IDC study sponsored by Kinaxis found only 2% of 2,000-plus supply-chain leaders report no AI capabilities, though just 6% call their chains "autonomous at scale" and 52% cite trust as the top barrier; 41% expect autonomous operations within one to two years. Logistics-AI tools such as Trimble's new "Arc Agent" aim to automate back-office transport work.

Industry Impact

Robotics and factory AI are both a growth market and a competitiveness lever for ACS. Every robot and humanoid needs adhesives, thermal-interface materials, potting compounds, conformal coatings and sealants — a rising, high-value demand stream tied directly to installation growth. Just as important, automated, AI-planned production lets chemical and materials makers cut cost, improve consistency and de-risk labour-short operations; the Kinaxis finding that trust and governance — not technology — are the main brakes suggests the winners will be those that operationalise AI in planning and quality, not just pilot it. China's lead in humanoid manufacturing and its push into European deployments also signal where the supplier relationships (and the materials specifications) will increasingly be set.

Business Day | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Xhby.net | China Economic Net | Financial Post | AP

item.title: Markets put the odds of a September US rate rise — the first in over three years — at 50-50 before key inflation data, as developed-world central banks turn hawkish and gold touched a record near $4,435 an ounce.
item.description:
The direction of interest rates has flipped from cuts to possible hikes. Traders now price a 50-50 chance the US Federal Reserve raises rates at its September meeting, which would be its first increase in more than three years, according to CME Group data — a move that would clash with President Trump's push for lower rates. The dollar traded sideways as markets awaited US inflation figures that will shape the decision. The shift is global: a Chinese survey notes major developed-economy central banks have moved from an easing bias to an overall "hawkish" stance under pressure from geopolitical conflict, AI-driven investment and wage dynamics — Australia has hiked three times this year, and the Bank of Japan, European Central Bank and Reserve Bank of New Zealand have each raised once, with more expected; only the Bank of Canada stays relatively dovish. Investors are hedging the uncertainty in precious metals: London spot gold hit a record near $4,435 an ounce (up 12.5% from its late-June low) and silver rose 21% from its July trough, lifting precious-metal ETFs sharply. Second-quarter corporate profits, meanwhile, were driven mainly by AI-related industries.

Industry Impact

Higher-for-longer or rising rates are a headwind for the interest-rate-sensitive end-markets that drive ACS demand — construction, housing, autos and industrial capex all cool when borrowing costs climb, and a stronger dollar can squeeze exporters and dollar-priced feedstock buyers. The hawkish turn also raises financing costs for chemical producers' own capital projects and working capital. Record gold and a hawkish Fed reflect a market bracing for war-driven, energy-led inflation to persist rather than fade — the same inflation that keeps ACS input costs elevated. Treasurers should plan for tighter, costlier financing and defend margins on the assumption that rate relief is further off than it looked a quarter ago.

AP | Business Recorder | China Economic Net | China Economic Net | Commercial Times

item.title: China's exports rose 23.9% in July, led by chips up 116.6% and ships up 92.4%, but a Tsinghua economist put real unemployment at 10.2% with fixed-asset investment down 4.1%, exposing a widening gap between a booming export machine and a weak home economy.
item.description:
China's July trade data underline a two-speed economy. Exports jumped 23.9% year-on-year in dollar terms, powered by integrated circuits up 116.6%, computers and components up 67.4%, ships up 92.4% and cars up 60.4% — evidence that Chinese manufacturers are capturing global share across both high-tech and heavy industry. Yet the domestic side looks fragile. Tsinghua University economist Li Daokui estimates China's real unemployment rate at 10.2%, with about 24 million people chronically underemployed, and notes fixed-asset investment fell 4.1% in January–May; he argues local governments have shifted from being the economy's engine to a drag, extracting taxes and arrears from firms rather than investing. Beijing is responding with supply-side and demand plans: the 30 July Politburo meeting pushed to expand domestic demand and move the "national unified market" — an effort to break down internal provincial trade barriers — into concrete implementation, while a "15th Five-Year Plan" urban-renewal programme is expected to drive CNY 15 trillion of investment, and Xi Jinping keeps championing "new quality productive forces" in AI and robotics. A separate report defends China's emerging industries against foreign claims that subsidies, not competitiveness, drive their success.

Industry Impact

For chemicals and ACS, the export surge and domestic weakness pull in opposite directions. Booming Chinese exports of chips, machinery, ships and cars sustain demand for the industrial adhesives, coatings and sealants embedded in those goods — but increasingly that demand is met by Chinese-made materials, deepening overcapacity pressure on Western producers in export markets. Meanwhile 10%-plus real joblessness and falling investment point to genuinely soft Chinese construction and consumer demand, capping volumes for building-and-consumer-facing ACS inside China. The CNY 15 trillion urban-renewal push is the key upside to watch: pipe networks, retrofits and housing upgrades are adhesive-, sealant- and coating-intensive, and could partly offset the property downturn if the money actually flows.

Hong Kong Commercial Daily | South China Morning Post | Bjd.com.cn | China Economic Net | China Economic Net | China Economic Net

item.title: China's passenger-car sales fell about 21% in July — a tenth straight monthly drop — even as electric and hybrid models hit a record 65% of sales, while exports jumped 88% to about 920,000 units and Western brands kept losing ground at home and in Europe.
item.description:
China's auto market is splitting in two. Domestic passenger-car sales fell about 21% year-on-year in July to roughly 1.47 million units, the tenth consecutive monthly decline, on weak consumer spending; sales for January–July were down 20.5%. New-energy vehicles — battery-electric and plug-in hybrids — set a record 65% of sales, but even they slipped 3.9% as buyers held back, while internal-combustion sales collapsed 41%. Unable to sell at home, manufacturers are pushing hard abroad: exports surged about 88% year-on-year to around 920,000 units in July, with plug-in and electric exports up nearly 148%. The contrast with Western incumbents is stark. General Motors is winding down Chevrolet sales in mainland China after selling just 36 cars there in six months, keeping only after-sales service for 7 million existing owners. Going the other way, Chinese brand Nio's registrations in Germany collapsed 93.6% in July to three units — a reminder that the export push is not yet translating into European traction for every brand. Globally, research house GlobalData expects hybrids, not pure EVs, to lead growth through 2035, with India, South America and Southeast Asia the fastest-growing hybrid markets.

Industry Impact

Autos are a major ACS demand pillar — structural adhesives, sealants, coatings and battery-assembly bonding all ride on where cars are built and sold. A tenth month of Chinese demand decline signals softer domestic volumes for auto-grade chemicals inside China, while the export surge shifts that demand to wherever Chinese OEMs assemble abroad, changing the geography of supply for ACS makers. The record NEV share keeps favouring battery-and-lightweighting chemistries over traditional formulations. Chevrolet's retreat and Nio's German stumble show a violent reshuffle of brands and plant footprints — ACS suppliers should follow the production shift (toward Chinese-owned capacity and new export hubs) rather than legacy nameplates, and note that the durable global growth may be in hybrids, which keep more combustion-related content than pure EVs.

Financial Post | Handelsblatt | The Standard | Commercial Times | South China Morning Post | Bloomberg

item.title: Germany's chemical industry raised its 2026 forecast as the Hormuz oil squeeze lifted prices and hurt Gulf-oil-dependent rivals — BASF's operating profit jumped 54% — while Covestro declared force majeure on the low Rhine, showing the war cuts both ways.
item.description:
For once the German chemical industry has good news, but it is fragile. Les Echos reports producers revised their 2026 outlook upward: the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz sent European pump prices higher yet also choked off Chinese competitors that depend heavily on Gulf oil and created bottlenecks that favour European supply. BASF, based in Ludwigshafen, pushed through significant price increases and lifted its adjusted quarterly operating profit 54% to €2.4 billion. The relief is uneven, though: Covestro declared force majeure — a clause that frees a supplier from delivery obligations because of events beyond its control — on selected products after record-low Rhine water levels disrupted its Dormagen site, which makes precursors for foams used in mattresses and refrigerators; it is switching to low-water vessels, road and rail but cannot fully offset the lost capacity. Feedstock signals are mixed elsewhere too: the Middle East nitrogen-fertilizer benchmark fell back to about $450 a tonne (half the April peak) after China approved some urea exports, but phosphate stays in crisis as war curtails sulphur supply. And demand pockets are healthy — premium acrylic "solid surface" materials are gaining share across Gulf and Indian commercial construction, a market projected to top $58 billion by 2032.

Industry Impact

This is Henkel's core operating environment, and today's picture is genuinely two-sided. The upward German forecast shows the war can be a margin tailwind for European producers when it disadvantages Asian rivals and supports pricing — a rare positive after months of "dying quietly" headlines. But Covestro's force majeure is a concrete reminder that the same conditions (a hot, dry summer and a stressed Rhine) can halt ACS-relevant output at any riverside site, tightening precursor supply for foams, coatings and adhesives. The steadier fertilizer/nitrogen benchmark eases one input, while resilient Gulf/India construction-materials demand points to where downstream ACS growth still lives. Net: capture pricing power where it exists, but keep low-water logistics and feedstock buffers ready — the tailwind and the shock come from the same source.

Les Echos | MarketScreener | IFDC | AP

item.title: Canada is racing to strike a deal before a 50% US tariff on about $20 billion of goods takes effect on 19 August, while the US government appealed a court order that would refund tariffs judged illegal to every importer, not just those that sued.
item.description:
Two tariff stories advanced at once. Canada's US-trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer for a third time in three weeks, aiming to put an interim deal to President Trump by 17 August — a day before a threatened 50% tariff on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods (about 5.2% of US imports from Canada) is due on 19 August. The list covers lumber, cement, furniture, wine, beer, spirits, and paper and cardboard; these would stack on existing US duties of 50% on steel and aluminium, 25% on autos and 10% on lumber. Separately, Washington asked the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit to overturn a ruling by a Court of International Trade judge that ordered Customs to refund tariffs judged illegal back in February to all importers — even those that never filed suit. The government argues the judge overstepped by applying the ruling universally, citing a 2025 Supreme Court decision that limited such broad "universal" remedies. About $100 billion in refunds has already been certified. Meanwhile the US separately imposed a new 12.5% tariff on Turkish olive oil (versus 10% on EU goods), a reminder the Section 301 "forced-labour" tariff regime — import taxes tied to how goods are made — keeps widening to individual products.

Industry Impact

Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) supply chains are directly exposed to both threads. A 50% Canada tariff would hit construction-linked materials — cement, lumber, wood furniture — that sit close to ACS end-markets, raising North American building-material costs and demand uncertainty just as the sector is soft. The refund fight matters for cash and precedent: companies that paid the February tariffs have a stake in whether refunds stand, and the appeal signals the administration will defend its tariff toolkit hard. For chemical and materials makers, the practical read is continued tariff volatility across North America — plan sourcing and pricing for duties staying on, not coming off, and watch the 17–19 August window closely.

La Presse | MarketScreener | The Globe and Mail | AP | AP | Dünya

item.title: US forces disabled a cargo ship breaking the Iran blockade and Houthi rebels killed six crew in the first merchant deaths of the war, driving oil to a two-week high near $89 as US–Iran talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz collapsed into impasse.
item.description:
The Iran war took a sharper turn at sea. A US Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Vela Nova, a Panama-flagged cargo ship, in the Gulf of Oman after it ignored warnings — the third vessel forcibly stopped since the US reimposed its blockade of Iran's ports on 14 July. Separately, Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck the small cargo ship Tihamah in two waves in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait (the chokepoint linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden), killing six — including rescue workers who had boarded after the first hit — and injuring ten. These are the first reported merchant-crew deaths since the war began in late February, and signal the conflict is spilling wider across the region. Diplomacy stalled: talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz reached an impasse, with Iran demanding sanctions relief, reparations and a ban on US and Israeli warships, and Washington refusing terms that let Tehran restrict shipping. Gulf energy producers increasingly treat Iran's control of the strait as permanent. Brent settled near $88.9, its highest since 31 July, after jumping about 5% the day before. Iran's own economy is buckling — July oil revenue near zero, inflation above 80% — but it is rationing to hold out.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, this war remains the single biggest swing factor for input costs. Forcible enforcement of the blockade and the first merchant deaths raise the risk premium on every cargo through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, keeping oil, naphtha, solvent and marine-freight prices elevated and headline-driven. The spread of attacks to the Red Sea threatens a second shipping artery for Europe–Asia trade, lengthening routes and lead times for feedstock and finished goods. With diplomacy stalled, producers should assume elevated, volatile energy costs into the autumn, keep hedges and buffer stocks in place, and treat single-day oil swings as noise until a Hormuz reopening is actually confirmed.

Daily Sabah | Arab News | Chinatimes | Business Recorder | CNA | LiveMint | Chinatimes
